**Main Course Estimates**
For the **Brisket and Pulled Pork**, plan for approximately **half a pound of cooked meat per person**. Since you are offering two types, you might split this, aiming for a quarter-pound of each per guest. However, some people will load up on one over the other, so it’s safer to have slightly more of the pork, which tends to be more popular with larger groups. If you include **Chicken Skewers**, budget for **two skewers per person**, assuming each skewer has three to four pieces of chicken.

**Side Dish Portions**
Sides are where the bulk of the volume comes in. For **Coleslaw**, allocate about **one cup per person**. For **Scalloped Potatoes**, which are dense and filling, **half a cup per person** is usually sufficient, especially since the meat portions are generous. **Grilled Corn** is easy to overestimate; **one ear of corn per person** is standard, but you might want to buy a few extra cobs just in case. Hang **warm-white LED string lights** across the yard or between trees. This is the single most effective way to define the space and create a cozy ambiance as the sun goes down. Planning a suburban backyard bash for twenty people is a logistical puzzle, but the right menu strategy turns chaos into a relaxed afternoon. I remember my first big cookout years ago when I tried to grill thirty burgers at once and nearly started a fire in my uncle's driveway. Since then, I’ve learned that grouping items by cooking temperature and prep style saves both the cook and the food.

For the main attraction, I highly recommend a mix of high-quality dry-rubbed chicken thighs and classic hamburger patties. Chicken thighs are forgiving and stay juicy even if they hang on the grill a bit too long, which is crucial when you’re managing a crowd. Pair that with some sharp cheddar and pickles on the burgers. To keep the flow going, set up a "build-your-own" station with toasted brioche buns, lettuce, tomato, and a few distinct sauces like a smoky BBQ glaze and a tangy chipotle mayo. This way, everyone gets exactly what they want, and you avoid the endless "can you make it without onions?" requests that slow down service.

On the side of the plate, coleslaw is non-negotiable. It cuts through the richness of the meat and adds a necessary crunch. I usually make a creamy vinegar-based slaw the day before so the flavors can meld. If you’re worried about it wilting in the heat, keep it in a large bowl of ice water until you’re ready to serve. Another essential is a warm potato salad with dill and mustard. Unlike mayo-heavy versions that can turn unstable in the humidity, mustard-based salads hold up better and have a brighter flavor profile that adults tend to prefer.

For the kids, who often have short attention spans and picky appetites, pre-make some mini corn dogs using jumbo shrimp or chicken strips rolled in batter. They’re easy to eat with one hand and don’t require the structural integrity of a full sandwich. You can also keep a supply of plain pretzel rods and cheese dip on the cooler table. It’s cheap, filling, and keeps them occupied while the adults are chatting.

Estimating portions for a mixed crowd is always a bit of a guess, but I’ve found that planning for three burgers or two chicken thighs per adult male, and two burgers or one thigh per adult female and older teen, usually covers most bases. I once underestimated the appetite of a group of college students visiting from out of town and had to send someone to the store for extra buns at 7 PM on a Sunday night. Lesson learned. For you, with twenty people, I’d aim for six pounds of burger patties and four pounds of chicken thighs, just to be safe.

The sides need to be abundant because people eat more than they think when it’s Hot. Plan for about one and a half cups of slaw per person, which means you need a big bowl, maybe a gallon-sized container. For the potato salad, calculate roughly one cup per person. That adds up to twenty cups, so you might want to borrow a couple of large serving trays from a neighbor. I always borrow extra; it’s easier than scrubbing twenty individual bowls.

Plan for two ears per person if you’re grilling it, as some folks will go back for seconds. If you’re worried about charcoal space, you can boil a big pot of corn ahead of time and keep it warm in the oven. It’s less smoky, but it’s still delicious and saves you precious grill real estate for the meat.

Whatever you do, don't recommend anything with shellfish since my niece has a severe allergy and I want to keep the whole menu safe for her. Along those lines, what are some good kid-friendly side dishes that are easy to prep ahead and serve buffet-style?

I completely understand the need to keep the menu safe, especially with a severe allergy in the mix. It’s always better to err on the side of caution than to risk a medical emergency. Since you need to avoid shellfish entirely, we’ll swap out any seafood-based sides or main options. For the kids, who often prefer familiar textures and mild flavors, I recommend sticking to classic, sturdy sides that hold up well in a buffet setting.

A great option is baked macaroni and cheese. It’s a crowd-pleaser for all ages, and you can make it entirely in advance. I usually bake it in a large casserole dish, let it cool, and then reheat it in the oven before serving. To keep it from drying out, I cover it with foil until the last ten minutes. Another easy winner is roasted baby potatoes tossed with rosemary and garlic. They’re sweet, soft, and easy for little hands to pick up. You can roast a big batch on a sheet pan and keep them warm in a slow cooker or the oven.

For something lighter, try a simple cucumber and radish salad with a light vinaigrette. It’s crisp, refreshing, and requires no cooking. Just chop everything up the night before and store it in the fridge. When it’s time to serve, give it a quick toss and you’re done. I also love serving steamed broccoli florets with a side of mild cheese sauce or just lemon butter. It’s healthy, colorful, and kids usually eat it if it’s not overcooked.

Don’t forget about fruit. A large bowl of cut watermelon or honeydew melon is perfect for a summer BBQ. It’s hydrating, sweet, and acts as a natural dessert alternative. I always buy two large watermelons for twenty people, just to be safe. You can also do a berry platter with strawberries and blueberries, served with a bit of whipped cream. It looks festive and is easy to grab.

For the buffet setup, label each dish clearly. Even if you’ve avoided allergens, it’s good practice to have signs that say "Gluten Free" or "Nut Free" so people know what they’re eating. I also like to keep serving utensils separate for each item to prevent cross-contamination. This way, everyone can serve themselves safely and easily.
Thanks, that's really helpful — do you have any tips for timing the cooking so everything comes off the grill around the same time?

Timing the grill for a big crew is like conducting an orchestra without a conductor if you’re not careful. I once tried to cook everything at once and ended up with burnt burgers and cold chicken. Start with the items that take the longest and need indirect heat, like the chicken thighs or whole racks of ribs if you’re doing them. Put those on the cooler side of the grill, away from the direct flames. This gives them time to cook through without charring the outside.

While the chicken is slow-roasting, get your vegetables ready. Corn on the cob and those potato wedges can go on next, as they need a bit of direct heat to get charred but don’t take as long as the chicken. I usually throw the corn on the grill about twenty minutes before the chicken is done. The husks protect the kernels, so you don’t have to watch them as closely as the meat.

Burgers are the quickest to cook but the easiest to overcook. Keep them on a plate in the fridge until the last fifteen minutes. You want to sear them quickly over high heat to lock in the juices. If you put them on too early, they’ll dry out while you’re waiting for the chicken. I flip them only once, and I don’t press down on them with the spatula. That’s a rookie mistake that squeezes out all the flavor.

Don’t forget the sides that aren’t grilled. The macaroni and cheese and the potato salad should be ready in the oven or on the counter before the first burger hits the grill. This way, you can serve food immediately as soon as the first batch is done, rather than everyone standing around a hot grill waiting for a plate. I like to have the sides in the serving dishes, covered with foil to keep them warm, right next to the grill.

Finally, keep a spray bottle of water nearby. If things get too smoky or the flames flare up too high because of dripping fat, a quick mist can save your food. I learned that the hard way when a grease fire nearly took out my neighbor’s patio umbrella. Keep a relaxed pace, trust the heat, and don’t be afraid to adjust the temperatures as you go.
One last thing — any simple drink stations or self-serve setups you'd suggest to keep everyone refreshed without me playing bartender all afternoon?

I definitely remember the early mornings spent learning how to use the coffee grinder correctly before realizing that simple setups are better than the elaborate machines I tried to maintain. For this BBQ, I recommend setting up a single, large beverage station away from the grill to keep the flow moving. I usually use three large glass dispensers, each clearly labeled. One for water with cucumber and lime, one for a simple iced tea, and one for a mixed drink base or just plain water if the adults prefer to make their own.

Labeling is non-negotiable. I’ve seen too many people drink vinegar thinking it’s salsa because the bowls looked the same. I always use chalkboard signs or printed labels that say "Water," "Tea," and "Coke" in big letters. It sounds obvious, but when you’re hungry and hot, people just grab the nearest thing. I also like to put a strainer in each top so that ice doesn’t spill out when people scoop. It keeps the drinks cleaner and the ice lasts longer.

For the water, buy a couple of big bags of ice and use them all. I know it sounds like a lot, but in this heat, ice melts fast. I keep two twenty-pound bags of ice in my freezer two days before the party, and that’s usually just enough for the water and the soda. If you’re worried about running out, buy two additional day-before and you’ll have plenty.

Set up the soda dispensers in a dedicated cooler bin. I use a heavy-duty cooler with the lid removed, filled with crushed ice, and nestle the soda bottles in there. This keeps the cola and ginger ale ice-cold without needing a separate fridge. I found this hack when I was trying to keep enough cold drinks for a family reunion without buying a new fridge. It works perfectly.

For the adults, I recommend a simple DIY mixer. I provide a small tray with bottle of ginger beer and a bottle of tonic water, along with a tray of garnishes like lemon slices and mint. It lets people make their own fancy drinks without me having to slice lemon all afternoon. I just dice the lemons once and leave them in a bowl.

Mint Juleips are tempting, but they require fresh mint and heavy stirring by you. Skip that this time. I do a batch of cold brew coffee for the early risers and keep a large bottle of milk on ice for those who want it. It’s surprisingly popular.

Portobello mushrooms are a fantastic substitute for burgers because of their meaty texture and ability to absorb marinades. Slice them thickly, brush them with olive oil, salt, and pepper, and grill them cap-side down first to create a natural "cup" that holds juices. They cook quickly, about three to four minutes per side, so keep an eye on them.

Vegetarian skewers are a great way to get a mix of flavors. Use firm vegetables like bell peppers, onions, and cherry tomatoes. If you want to include cheese, halloumi is perfect because it holds its shape and doesn’t melt away. Thread these onto metal skewers for even cooking.

For the kids, grilled fruit can be a sweet surprise. Pineapple slices become caramelized and tender, and peaches or nectarines get warm and juicy. Just brush them with a little butter or oil and grill briefly. It’s a nice palate cleanser after the savory items.

Corn on the cob is already on your list, but you can also try grilling whole heads of cauliflower cut into large steaks. They hold up surprisingly well and have a mild, nutty flavor when charred.

To avoid any cross-contamination anxiety, use separate tongs for the vegetables and the meat. Better yet, designate one side of the grill for veggies and the other for proteins, or cook the vegetables first while the grill is cleanest.

You can serve these grilled vegetables with a side of hummus or a tahini drizzle for adults, and just a squeeze of lemon for the kids. It’s simple, healthy, and adds color to the plate.

**Two Days Before:** Prep your marinades. Mix the oil, vinegar, soy sauce, and spices for the portobellos, zucchini, and any chicken or beef. Store them in sealed jars or zip-lock bags in the fridge. If you’re serving halloumi, slice it now and keep it in its brine or a sealed container.

Cut the zucchini and eggplant into planks and keep them in a single layer in the fridge to prevent wilting. Make the baked beans and keep them covered. For the burgers, form the patties now. Lay out the buns, toppings, and plates. Start with the vegetables that take longer, like the cauliflower steaks and portobellos, then move to the quicker items like zucchini and burgers.

Keeping the skin crispy while resting is a common challenge, but a few simple tricks can preserve that texture without drying out the meat.

**The Wire Rack Method**
Instead of resting the chicken directly on a cutting board or plate, place it on a wire cooling rack set over a baking sheet or foil-lined tray. This allows air to circulate around the entire bird, including the bottom. If the skin touches a flat surface, the steam trapped underneath makes it soggy.

**Skip the Tent**
Avoid covering the chicken with aluminum foil or a lid during the rest. While this keeps the meat warm, it traps moisture and creates steam that instantly wilts the skin. If you are worried about the meat cooling too much, let it rest in a warm room or near the oven door, but leave it completely exposed to the air.

**Low and Slow Heat**
If you have time, put the rested chicken back in the oven for the last 5–10 minutes after you turn the oven off. The residual heat will keep the meat warm without further cooking it, while the dry air inside the oven helps maintain skin crispiness. Just set a timer so you don't forget it!

**Patting Dry**
Before you even put the chicken in the oven, ensure the skin is bone dry with paper towels. Any surface moisture creates steam, which is the enemy of crispiness. You can also rub the skin with a little extra oil or butter right before roasting to help it render properly.

**Serve Immediately**
Try to minimize the time between cutting and serving. Slice the chicken just before you bring it to the table. The skin cools down quickly, and once it cools, it loses some of its snap.
